item.title: OpenAI argues for using perplexity as a shared metric to track AI model progress and establish industry safety standards [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: OpenAI's Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki explains that perplexity, a measure of how well AI models predict data, is a key indicator of AI progress and emerging capabilities. The company has published internal perplexity data to promote transparency and encourage a common framework for evaluating AI development across the industry. The article outlines how improvements in perplexity have correlated with significant advances in AI capabilities, from GPT-2's coherent text generation to GPT-4's reasoning skills and recent breakthroughs in cybersecurity and mathematics. Pachocki emphasizes that while downstream benchmarks evolve rapidly, perplexity remains a stable and informative metric for tracking the underlying intelligence of AI models. OpenAI also discusses the accelerating role of AI in its own development, particularly in algorithmic research on pretraining, which could lead to faster progress. The company views establishing perplexity as a shared standard as a step toward coordinated safety measures and a scientific basis for pacing future AI advancements.

item.title: Analysis finds Anthropic's US data centers will rely on 87% gas and 11% coal power by 2028, with no direct renewable energy commitments [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Anthropic's planned data centers in the US are expected to be predominantly powered by fossil fuels, with about 87% of energy from gas and 11% from coal by 2028, according to a recent analysis. The company has made no direct commitments to renewable energy in the US, although it has renewable contracts in Norway and Canada. This reliance on fossil fuels could result in significant carbon emissions, potentially exceeding those of California's power generation in 2028. The analysis highlights the environmental impact of AI data center expansion and the limited adoption of renewable energy sources in this sector.

item.title: Developer releases Worker 755, a browser game where players act as subagents to AI managers using real LLMs like Claude and GPT [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Worker 755 is a browser-based game in which players take on the role of a subagent managed by an AI agent powered by large language models such as Claude, GPT, Gemini, and others. The AI manager assigns tasks with a time limit, evaluates player performance, and provides feedback, simulating a workplace environment where the player must complete or report on assigned commands. The game supports free shifts on servers with shared keys or paid shifts using personal API keys from OpenRouter or Vercel AI Gateway, ensuring privacy by only sending keys to the game server during active shifts. It offers configurable options including sandbox or live database modes, scripted or AI-driven managers, and various AI models for the player role. The project is open source, runs on Node.js, and includes detailed setup instructions and Docker support.

item.title: Graham Dumpleton launches Muru, an AI-assisted Rust server for running ASGI and WSGI Python apps in development and production [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Graham Dumpleton, creator of mod_wsgi, has developed Muru, a new AI-assisted Rust server designed to serve Python web applications using ASGI and WSGI protocols. Muru aims to provide improved tools for both development and production environments. Dumpleton has documented the project's progress extensively over several weeks, sharing detailed insights into its architecture, features, and integration with technologies like Kubernetes. The project reflects two decades of experience with mod_wsgi and incorporates AI assistance to enhance server management and deployment.

item.title: OpenAI urges leading AI developers to agree on limits for AI development until behavior can be better understood and monitored [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: OpenAI's chief scientist has called on major AI companies to establish agreed-upon limits on AI development to ensure responsible progress. The proposal emphasizes setting industry standards to define initial boundaries on AI advancement until sufficient understanding and monitoring of AI behavior are in place.

item.title: Taskless launches deterministic rule engine to convert AGENTS.md and PR comments into runnable code checks without AI in the loop [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Taskless introduces a tool that transforms agent harness rules written in markdown or PR comments into deterministic, testable code checks that run consistently without relying on AI models. The open-source CLI runs locally without requiring an account, supporting over 25 languages and integrating with linters and GitHub for scalable enforcement. The system compiles user-defined rules into syntax tree or prose-based checks, ensuring the same result every time and eliminating the need to maintain AGENTS.md or skills directories. Taskless Cloud offers additional runtime rules and team-wide integrations, with the project recently surpassing 200,000 successful checks since May 2026. Taskless aims to improve code quality by automating rule enforcement based on team decisions rather than AI opinions, allowing corrections to compound over time and reduce manual code review overhead.

item.title: Strict launches software to run GitHub Actions CI on spare Macs and Linux boxes with zero-sudo setup and auto load-balancing
item.description: Strict offers a tool that enables developers to run continuous integration workflows on spare Mac or Linux machines using GitHub Actions runners. The software operates alongside GitHub's official runner over Tailscale, providing features like auto load-balancing, warm NVMe caching, and self-healing to optimize resource use and reduce cloud CI costs. Users can enroll spare Macs or Linux hosts with minimal setup and no open ports, running workflows directly from GitHub over HTTPS. Strict supports seamless integration with existing workflows by swapping the runs-on parameter, and it includes monitoring, alerts, and automatic cleanup to minimize maintenance. Additionally, users can contribute idle Mac hardware to the Strict Network to run sandboxed builds and earn payouts while retaining priority for their own jobs.

item.title: MIT launches Processor Database compiling decades of CPU and GPU data to support AI-era hardware research and development [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: MIT has introduced the Processor Database, a comprehensive resource tracking the evolution of CPUs and GPUs over time to aid researchers, engineers, and industry leaders in understanding hardware trends amid the end of Moore's Law. The database builds on Stanford's earlier CPU Database, updating and expanding it with modern processors and plans to include FPGAs and AI-specific chips, along with benchmark performance data. This tool aims to provide critical insights for designing new chips and studying computing progress in the AI era, addressing a gap left by outdated resources and supporting informed hardware decisions.

item.title: OpenAI chief scientist proposes using perplexity as a benchmark to limit AI development speed amid calls for common safety standards [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: OpenAI's chief scientist Jakub Pachocki outlined a proposal to use perplexity-a measure of how well AI models predict text-as a standard metric to gauge and potentially limit the pace of AI development. This comes amid industry discussions about slowing AI progress to address safety and existential risks highlighted by former researchers and company filings. Pachocki argues that traditional benchmarks quickly become outdated as AI capabilities evolve, but perplexity remains a consistent indicator of model performance. He suggests that AI companies could agree on perplexity thresholds to pause development until better understanding and monitoring of AI behavior are achieved, supporting recent calls from Anthropic's CEO and endorsements from OpenAI and SpaceX leadership for common safety standards and pacing AI advancements.

item.title: Guide to running local AI models Inkling, Qwen, and Unsloth on Windows PCs with GPUs, focusing on privacy and cost benefits over cloud AI [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: This article explains how to set up local AI models like Inkling, Qwen, and Unsloth on a Windows PC with a GPU, enabling private, cost-effective AI use at home without cloud dependencies. It highlights the benefits of local AI, including avoiding usage limits and privacy concerns associated with cloud providers like OpenAI and Anthropic. The guide details hardware requirements, model selection based on GPU VRAM, and the use of quantization to fit large models on consumer-grade GPUs. It provides practical advice for beginners to install and run these models using Unsloth Desktop, emphasizing simplicity and accessibility for home users.

item.title: Etsy sellers shut down shops in response to new AI content policy changes
item.description: Many Etsy sellers have closed their shops following the platform's introduction of a new AI policy that affects how AI-generated content is handled. The policy changes have sparked concern among creators about the impact on their businesses and the authenticity of listings. Sellers cite the new rules as a reason for their departure, highlighting tensions between the platform's AI regulations and the seller community's practices.

item.title: Analysis: AI experts' superintelligence predictions align with rapid AI progress and breakthroughs in 2025-2026 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Many AI researchers and rationalist communities predict imminent recursive self-improvement leading to superintelligence that could transform society rapidly. This perspective is supported by accelerating AI capabilities, including AI systems solving complex mathematical problems and discovering software vulnerabilities in 2025 and 2026. The article discusses responsible AI skepticism that acknowledges rapid AI progress without dismissing current capabilities or assuming human cognition is uniquely irreproducible. It highlights that while skepticism exists, recent AI achievements and forecasting accuracy lend credibility to the superintelligence outlook, suggesting it may be directionally correct despite ongoing debate.

item.title: Amazon develops a 4.4-gigawatt AI data center campus in Pennsylvania, repurposing a former coal plant to support large-scale AI infrastructure beyond the reach of smaller cloud providers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Amazon is transforming a 4.4-gigawatt site in Pennsylvania, formerly a coal-fired power plant, into one of the largest AI data center campuses in the US. The project involves converting a Rust Belt industrial relic into a modern facility with 36 buildings powered by gas-fired electricity to support AI workloads for companies like Anthropic. This development highlights Amazon's ability to invest heavily in long-term, large-scale infrastructure that smaller cloud providers, often supported by Nvidia, struggle to match. The site reflects a shift in the tech industry toward securing dedicated AI infrastructure in regions with available power and economic challenges.

item.title: Anthropic founders Dario and Daniela Amodei aim to preserve the company's unconventional AI research approach amid IPO plans [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Dario and Daniela Amodei, siblings and co-founders of AI research company Anthropic, are focused on maintaining the firm's unique and creative approach to artificial intelligence development. They emphasize innovation and a distinctive culture as they prepare for the company's upcoming IPO. Their leadership seeks to balance growth with preserving the company's original vision and experimental ethos.

item.title: SHL research finds nearly 20% of US workers replaced by AI were asked to return, with most demanding pay raises, job security, and transparency
item.description: A survey by talent assessment company SHL reveals that nearly one in five American workers who were replaced by AI were subsequently invited back by their employers. These returning workers commonly request substantial pay increases, guarantees of future job security, and clear information about how AI will be used alongside them. The study, conducted in mid-2026 with over 2,000 respondents in the US and UK, highlights a phenomenon SHL calls "AI rebounding," where companies realize the value of human workers only after replacing them with software. The survey also shows that most workers are willing to adapt to AI-driven changes rather than leave their jobs, with nearly half preferring retraining over job loss. However, the demands for better pay and transparency indicate that organizations often underestimate employee contributions and fail to communicate AI's role effectively. SHL suggests that companies should assess and develop internal talent more rigorously instead of relying solely on external hiring to fill skill gaps.

item.title: TheGitAI launches CLI agent for Linux supporting computer control on Wayland and X11 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: TheGitAI has released a command-line interface agent that enables direct computer control on Linux systems using both Wayland and X11 display servers. This tool operates applications beyond file and shell command management, enhancing automation and user interaction on Linux and macOS, with similar functionality on Windows 11. The agent can run on the user's screen or a separate background screen and is accessible via both CLI and desktop applications under the same account, providing a unified experience across platforms.

item.title: Flowframes launches free AI app to increase video frame rates up to 120 FPS using local GPU processing [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Flowframes has released a free AI-powered application that enhances video smoothness by increasing frame rates from 24 or 30 FPS to 60, 120, or custom rates using advanced interpolation models like RIFE. The software processes videos locally on Windows 10 and 11 PCs with Nvidia, AMD, or Intel GPUs, generating new frames that preserve motion clarity for films, animations, gameplay, and AI-generated content. The app supports common video formats and image sequences, offering features such as intelligent frame de-duplication, scene detection, and multiple AI models for interpolation. It is designed for video editors, animators, and gamers who want smoother motion and cleaner slow-motion effects without rebuilding projects frame by frame.

item.title: OpenAgentCore launches open-source, self-hosted implementation of OpenAI Agents API compatible with Codex, Claude Code, and MiniMax Code models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: OpenAgentCore is an open-source project that provides a self-hosted version of the OpenAI Agents API, allowing users to run AI agents like Codex, Claude Code, or MiniMax Code on their own machines using the official OpenAI SDK. It supports multiple operating systems and offers modular components such as sandbox providers and model providers for customization. The platform maintains durable execution state and enables flexible deployment with features like pausing idle sandboxes and resuming workspaces on compatible nodes. Installation is supported via Docker on Linux and macOS, with a PowerShell script for Windows, and it integrates seamlessly with existing OpenAI SDK workflows by setting environment variables for API base URL and keys.

item.title: Pieter Levels releases tool to block 3,728 X accounts posting automated AI replies, aiming to create a network-wide block [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Pieter Levels published a list of 3,728 X accounts he identifies as posting automated AI replies and released a tool that lets users block all these accounts at once. He hopes widespread use will turn his account into a honeypot for AI replies, effectively blocking these accounts from replying to anyone across the network. Levels has also shared the list with X's CEO to help train spam detection models. The tool includes a browser agent prompt that automates blocking at a rate of one account every 3 to 5 seconds, with a recommendation to use Claude's Chrome extension. Levels requires accounts appealing their block to swear an oath never to use AI for public replies again, warning that breaking this oath will result in a permanent block. The list includes evidence for each account, though flags are based on judgment calls rather than definitive proof of AI use.

item.title: AnonimusShamshiAlex releases FLEY AI-Voice assistant and FLEY Glasses 1.0 smart glasses with integrated AI on ESP32-S3 microcontroller [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: AnonimusShamshiAlex has released FLEY AI-Voice, a free AI assistant available on Windows, Linux, and Android, along with FLEY Glasses 1.0, smart glasses featuring an integrated AI assistant powered by an ESP32-S3 microcontroller. The glasses recognize voice commands, analyze real-time video to assess threats, save photos to a memory card, and provide audio responses through built-in speakers. The projects are open source and available on GitHub, with additional information and downloads accessible via the developer's website and Telegram channel.

item.title: How Apple Got Caught Up in Google Search Ads Slowdown [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Google's shares have fallen 18% since the company reported a sharp slowdown in search advertising revenue growth stemming in part from the increased popularity of its AI features. Google isn't the only tech company feeling the pain from that shift. Growth in Apple's services revenue, which includes a cut of ad revenue Google makes when people search on Apple's Safari web browser, slowed to 10% in the latest quarter from 12% in the prior quarter, and will cool further in the current quarter, executives said on Apple's earnings call earlier this month. Reddit also warned in its latest quarterly report that Google wasn't sending as much search referral traffic to its online forums because of AI-driven changes to search features.

item.title: Can Jensen Really Return?
item.description: Welcome, Weekenders! Jensen Huang wants a mulligan, and a good number of people seem keen to let him have one. On Tuesday, just days after the longtime Nvidia CEO resigned the job, Huang said in a statement he'd be open to taking back the job. Depending on your perspective, that suggestion is akin to letting a skunked dog back into bed-or a veritable Second Coming. For now, Nvidia's board is holding firm and has continued to insist it won't rehire Huang. One of the most prominent calls for Huang's return came on Friday, with President Donald Trump saying he thought Nvidia should give Huang his job back. "We're a country of second chances," Trump said. "He's a man ... who made some bad decisions." (Surely a situation Trump himself could understand.) In addition to Trump, a good number of industry pooh-bahs have continued to voice support for their fallen comrade and advocating for Huang was definitely a major topic on this week's very busy conference circuit. That support came in both implicit and explicit terms. At the New York Times' DealBook Summit, Elon Musk was blunt, saying "there's no one who can really replace" Huang. At the TomorrowX conference, former Uber CEO Travis Kalanick and Musk groupie Antonio Gracias donned black leather jackets to show their solidarity. And during a Semafor shindig in San Francisco, Sam Altman described Huang as a personal hero, Jeff Bezos said he was a "remarkable guy" and investor Bill Ackman labeled him as "one of the most iconic CEOs of all time." On X, Ackman has been theorizing about how Huang could actually return. Ackman (and venture capitalist Garry Tan) has been trumpeting a roundabout plan that involves getting together a 15% ownership block of Nvidia to call a special shareholder meeting and then ... vote out the anti-Huang board members ... and swing the board to a pro-Huang majority? It's somewhat unclear. (Apparently, Huang still has some allies on the board; remember, we told you that the board hadn't initially wanted to act at all.) "Ackman's idea is somewhere between extremely unlikely and remote," said Jeffrey Gordon, a Columbia University law professor and former Treasury Department attorney. (Or, in other words, as likely as defrosting a 20-pound Thanksgiving turkey overnight.) The proposal does seem to assume Huang supporters could really rile up Wall Street institutions with major Nvidia stakes, such as BlackRock, and get them to go activist-not a certain thing at all. It also conveniently ignores how difficult the math for a board-ousting vote looks when factoring in how much institutional money is held in passive-investing funds, which will never throw support behind an insurrection. Rather than a board coup, Huang's clearest route to returning would be if the board caves and changes its mind. Sure, it might, eventually. But we have to get through the many, many inquiries into Huang and Nvidia that have popped up and who knows what else we'll learn in the meantime, especially since there are a lotttt of people newly determined to peer into every Nvidia crevice: journalists galore, the SEC, the Commerce and Justice Departments, a trio of Congressional committees and possibly the FBI. The Huang situation keeps getting likened to Altman's ouster from OpenAI in 2023, which obviously ended with Altman's return. I don't think the comparison holds up. Most obviously, OpenAI was a private company-its board had more freedom to change its mind. And as Gordon pointed out to me, Altman's reinstatement came after a true mass rebellion of OpenAI staff: roughly 745 out of 770 employees signed a letter threatening to go with Altman to Microsoft, more than 95% of the company. Now, a letter supporting Huang's reinstatement is floating around the internet, and it purports to have signatures from 10,263 Nvidia employees. Even if they were all legit signatures, they represent only a quarter of the company's workforce. Maybe most Nvidians, as they call themselves, actually didn't like Huang's rampant humiliation tactics, which reportedly once included a threat to scalp someone and piss on their brain. Maybe most of them are comfortable living without him. I mean, sure, I'd totally get why!-Abram Brown (abe@theinformation.com) The Information's Must-Read Stories Nvidia Introduced Alibaba to Alice Huang for Workaround on U.S. Export Controls Jensen Huang's Right-Hand Man Oversaw Chip Customers-Including Alice Huang To Strengthen OpenAI, Brockman Goes 'Full Management Mode' 'Theranos But Real': New Blood-Testing Startup Says It Can Predict Health Risks Listening: "Stories of Art" After weeks like the ones we've just had, I like to make it a point to visit a museum and spend some time staring at ancient, beautiful things-a chance to relish the creative ingenuity of humans who never once heard the phrase "forward-deployed engineer." Truthfully, though, the tech action has lately been so fast-paced that I still haven't gotten to make one of those pilgrimages, so I've been counterprogramming my brain with a binge through "Stories of Art," a podcast about, yes, art-from Renaissance Florence to Basquiat's lower Manhattan loft-that launched earlier in the year. (Apple recently declared it one of 2026's best.) The hosts are a pair of amiable Brits, art historian James Fox and art critic Alastair Sooke, who take a cheerful, conversational approach to what might otherwise be dry recountings. In effect, they are to Renoir what "The Rest Is History" lads are to the Romans. (Given the subject matter of "Stories of Art"-namely, art-I suggest you watch the podcast's video version when you can. While Fox and Sooke are quite adept at describing the artworks they mention, it's nice to actually see what they're talking about.) Nearly all the artists who get mentioned achieved their fame through real entrepreneurial verve, challenging the entrenched status quo. (Sounds like a familiar motivation, right?) Take Claude Monet and the birth of Impressionism: The movement traces its origins to a decision in 1874 by Monet and a group of other artists to refuse to exhibit their work at an established gallery. Instead, they formed their own company (yes, founder mode Monet!) and then set up their own Paris exhibition space that featured newfangled technology, such as elevators. Many of you will enjoy one of the most recent episodes on James Whistler, a fellow who took a real dim view of journalists and pursued a high-profile libel lawsuit against one critic. A warning about how that turned out for Whistler: He did triumph in court. He then promptly went bankrupt.-Abram Brown Reading: "Fruit Fly" by Josh Silver In suburban north London, author Mallory Maddox seems to have a rich, full life: a handsome Netflix-executive husband, a townhome with $2,000 armchairs and dusky-pink walls and a literary world standing as a "modern-day Virginia Woolf," as one reviewer has christened her. Yet appearances are almost always deceiving in "Fruit Fly," a spry, tart satire of sex and 21st century storytelling: Mallory's relationship with hubbie Ronan has turned stiff and chilly, and as much as he thinks about the bedroom, it's to insist that it's time for kids. ("I haven't had an orgasm in years," she recalls in an ongoing inner monologue.) Professionally, Mallory is dogged by "a shadowy, persisting darkness"-a profound case of writer's block. To fill the time, she moonlights as an online therapist and hunts exhaustively for those expensive home furnishings. Desperate for writerly inspiration, she peruses Reddit-uh oh-and takes to heart another author's comment about the state of the publishing industry: "go dark, go gay." She downloads Grindr, sets up an account with a few of her husband's nudes and scores an invite to an orgy at a house down the street. She never actually sets foot inside but nevertheless makes the acquaintance of Leo, an attractive but homeless and drug-addicted gay man who sells himself to other men. (As the novel shifts perspectives, Leo contributes his own inner thoughts, which are often mordant and felonious. "Old women carry cash. Everyone knows that," he thinks, snatching a purse. "Someone should tell them to stop.") Mallory offers to counsel Leo-pro bono, bless her-and begins writing a novel that lightly fictionalizes his frayed life. For a time, he believes she's just a daffy do-gooder. ("This is weird," Leo thinks as she leads him through a silent-breathing exercise. "This is very fucking weird, but I guess I've done weirder things.") And her publishers absolutely adore what she is finally putting on the page. As one editor remarks: "It's so bleak-but also somehow so funny?" Much the same can be said about "Fruit Fly" itself.-A.B. Watching: "The Weight" President Franklin Roosevelt attempted to govern Depression-era America through no small number of novel schemes: A good many of them are quite famous, such as Social Security. A few have disappeared into history, including Roosevelt's 1933 executive order that banned gold hoarding, forcing Americans to turn over large stockpiles of the precious metal. (No one could keep more than $100 worth.) That presidential decision is the inciting force in "The Weight," a tense wilderness thriller starring Ethan Hawke as Murphy, leader of a group of convicts hired by their jailer (Russell Crowe) to heist a gold mine's reserves. It's part of a plan that's complex in the same way that "Goldfinger" is not actually a film about robbing Fort Knox. Often, heist films are fabulous capers, with champagne, tuxedos and bon mots. "The Weight" very much is not, depicting a bloodied-knuckled trek across the Oregon backwoods, with Murphy and his thieves weighed down, literally, by their bullion-filled backpacks and, metaphorically, by their past misdeeds and inner demons. Still, Murphy is well incentivized to make it through. In a true miscarriage of justice, he has been separated from his plucky daughter, Penny (Avy Berry); part of his reward for orchestrating the robbery is early release, which will let him reclaim her. "The Weight" does take a moment to get going. Then it really rips, with a pair of memorable fight scenes that are a real credit to both the film's editing and cinematography.-A.B.

item.title: How Anthropic Upstaged OpenAI on Road to Blockbuster IPO [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: On a sunny day in San Francisco last month, Anthropic Chief Financial Officer Krishna Rao and other executives huddled in the company's downtown headquarters to brief major investors on its latest financials-and assuage concerns. Revenue growth in the third quarter had fallen from its torrid pace. Privately, some investors doubted that the company could go public at the $1.5 trillion valuation bandied about for months, especially as AI-related stocks took a beating. Throughout the month, Rao and his squad countered those concerns by highlighting growth opportunities in fields from life sciences to chip design, say people familiar with the conversations. As for the broader market's jitters? Ignore it, they told investors. That turned out to be decent advice: By Thursday's close, Anthropic was worth $1.76 trillion on a fully diluted basis.
